activity.title: Shipping the CRM Agent in Surface today. The interesting part is that it treats CRM maintenance as a continuous decision problem, not a sync. Most CRM automation is plumbing. It moves fields between systems when a trigger fires, but nobody is deciding what should actually change. So the underlying problem never gets solved: records still go stale, contacts stay half-filled, deals sit in the wrong stage because a human never got to them. You've automated the moving of data, not the judgment about it. This matters because everything downstream inherits the quality of the CRM underneath it. Routing, scoring, forecasting, reporting all read from that data. When reps fall behind on upkeep, and they always do, the decay propagates into every system that depends on it. We built an agent that does the deciding. It runs as a reconciliation loop, not an event handler. It reads the current state, compares it against what the underlying activity implies should be true, and only acts on the gaps it can justify. A call happened but wasn't logged, so log it. A contact is missing a firmographic we already have, so fill it. A deal has had no activity in 40 days but sits in a stage that implies momentum, so flag or move it. The hard part was doing this safely against a live CRM a whole team depends on. Every action is written with provenance, so it corrects records without overwriting what a human deliberately set, and you can always see what changed and why. An agent that silently rewrites your CRM is worse than the problem it solves. It plugs into HubSpot and Salesforce. The effect is that your CRM's data quality stops being a function of how disciplined your reps were this week. ...more

Shipping ad analytics in Surface today. The technically interesting part is what makes it different from bolting on another reporting layer. The core problem with ad attribution isn't tooling, it's incentive structure. Ad platforms report on their own performance. They're graded on volume, optimized to show you signals that justify continued spend, and architecturally isolated from what actually happens to a lead after the click. You can run a campaign for months that looks healthy by platform metrics while the leads it generates are low intent, wrong ICP, or churning early. The platform never sees that signal. It keeps optimizing toward more of the same. The fix isn't another dashboard. It's closing the loop at the data layer. Because Surface runs lead capture, enrichment, and content performance on a single system, we can tie every ad dollar back to actual lead quality as it's being scored. Not after a quarterly attribution audit. When a lead converts, decays, or disqualifies, that signal propagates back to the spend data immediately. The data isn't crossing a gap between disconnected systems, it lives in one place. We also added industry and ICP benchmarking using anonymized peer data. Knowing your cost per lead in a vacuum tells you almost nothing. Knowing whether that number is out of range for companies selling to the same buyer is a different question. The hard part was making benchmarks useful without being misleading. Bucketing by ICP and industry required enough signal density per segment to be meaningful, and we're careful about where we have that and where we don't. What this unlocks is earlier course correction. You can know whether an ad is working 70-80% faster than waiting for downstream revenue data to confirm what the platform already obscured. That compression matters most in the first weeks of a new campaign, when the decisions about scaling or killing spend are still reversible. ...more

We just shipped the Surface Direct Scheduler. The scheduling itself isn't the interesting part, it's that routing decisions are now made by the same data layer that already knows which rep closes which ICP, what territory the lead came from, and where that account is in the funnel. Most scheduling tools route by availability. This one routes by likelihood of the meeting actually mattering. Tools like Calendly and Chili Piper price per seat, so every rep you hire increases your software spend before they've closed anything. And because those tools live outside your CRM, the routing logic is usually just round robin or a rule set someone configured six months ago. We built scheduling that lives natively on the platform with flat pricing. The routing engine pulls from the same signals already powering lead scoring and content targeting and makes the assignment the moment a meeting is booked. The hard part was making that fast enough to feel normal while running against live data. There's real tension between query depth and the sub-second response a booking flow demands. Customers cut around 50% of scheduling spend when they switch. But the real unlock is the feedback loop, when scheduling is connected to the same system scoring your leads, it closes in a way disconnected tools structurally can't. ...more

We shipped a research agent at Surface this week. Every lead that enters the system gets automatically researched the moment it arrives and the output lands as structured columns in the record before a rep ever opens it. The core engineering problem was timing. Research that completes after a rep already opened the record is useless, so the trigger had to fire at ingestion. Getting the output right was harder than the retrieval. Every company that comes through a pipeline looks different from the outside, some have tons of public data and others have almost nothing, and the agent has to produce a consistent structured output regardless of what it finds. That normalization work took more iteration than the actual research logic. Reps used to spend a few minutes before every call pulling context from Google, LinkedIn, Crunchbase. Nobody flags that as a problem because it's just what good prep looks like, but across a full week of pipeline it adds up to 5+ hours per rep. We're still tuning the tradeoff between depth and latency. A person doing research knows what actually matters for a specific deal and the agent doesn't have that judgment yet, but we built the schema around signals that historically convert and there's a version of this where conversion data feeds back into the research layer and sharpens it over time. ...more

i've been at surface labs longer than i was at snowflake now. 2.5 years there, 3 years here. at snowflake i worked on signup.snowflake.com , data marketplace, and accounts infrastructure. all different systems, all teaching me the same thing: don't build services that depend on someone else's data unless you absolutely have to. snowflake had a high bar for introducing anything new into the stack and that discipline is what made things stable at scale. when saharsh and i started surface, that thinking came with me. we built our own workflows, our own routing, our own forms. not because it was faster. because if we rented those primitives we wouldn't own the data running through them. every architectural decision at snowflake that stuck with me was about control and knowing exactly what your system does when things break. 3 years in and i'm not applying old lessons anymore. the snowflake experience gave me a foundation but surface is a different problem. we're building something that didn't exist before and the decisions i'm making now come from a mix of what i learned there and what i've had to figure out here. the longer tenure just means the balance shifted. more surface thinking, less snowflake thinking. that's probably how it should work. ...more

most form tools count completed submissions. we think that's the wrong metric. someone fills out 3 of 5 fields and leaves. most tools call that a failure. but they gave you a name, an email, maybe a company. that's not nothing. we built surface to capture those partial responses and route them into workflows just like completed ones. nurture sequences, sales alerts, CRM syncs. the data isn't perfect but it's real. the thing we didn't expect is that partial response capture ended up being our best churn predictor. customers who actually use it barely leave. the ones who only care about completed submissions churn way more often. when you think about it, it makes sense. most people don't finish forms. that's not a bug, that's just how people behave on the internet. if your tool only works when someone completes every field, you're throwing away most of your traffic. our stickiest customers figured this out on their own honestly. they stopped treating incomplete as junk and started treating it as a different kind of lead. less qualified, sure. but still worth a follow up. we used to care about form completion rates. now we care about what happens to every response regardless of whether someone finished or not. ...more

Most startup CTOs are optimizing for the wrong constraint. They're worried about language choice, architecture, build times, React vs Vue. Meanwhile the actual constraint is talking to customers. We have 2 engineers in San Francisco and 7 in India. The thing that moves the needle isn't code quality or tech stack. It's engineers who talk to customers and make decisions based on what they hear. When an engineer only codes and never talks to customers, they're building in a vacuum. They guess at what matters. They ship features nobody wants. But when an engineer knows the customer, knows what's breaking, they ship the right thing first time. That's the actual constraint. Not the technology. We hire for this now. We don't ask about your favorite framework or opinions on microservices. We ask if you can talk to a customer and make a decision based on what you hear. Most people can't. They want the customer to come with a fully articulated problem. The customer doesn't work that way. They say "this is annoying" and the engineer has to figure out what they mean. That's a skill. That's the constraint. Everyone's building faster now because AI made coding faster. Everyone's got the same tools. The companies that win are the ones where the engineer is closest to the problem. Stop optimizing your language. Start optimizing for listening. ...more

We're seeing a clear pattern in candidates we want to move forward with. Career changers keep winning over resume optimizers. One candidate spent five years in accounting. Quit their job to learn computer science. Built an app and spent over 100 hours on it with real customers. Then built something else because they couldn't stop. Another candidate had the perfect pedigree. Co-op program, internships at the right companies, all the boxes checked. Built something on the side with ten users and zero revenue. The difference is obvious when you see it. Career changers are fundamentally different from resume optimizers. When someone switches paths, that decision costs something. You don't make that move for optics. The accountant spent five years in a different field, then learned to code from scratch. No coasting on credentials. No relying on a brand name. Just commitment. We've seen this pattern repeatedly in strong candidates. Someone who took a grad-level class as a freshman even though they weren't allowed in, just emailed the professor anyway. Someone else who studied statistics and CS as a minor and built a project with 3K monthly users out of pure curiosity. These aren't traditional paths. They're people who decided what they wanted and went after it sideways. The resume optimizers follow the playbook. The career changers build their own. When you're evaluating someone who switched paths, you're looking at someone who's already proven they can learn, commit, and execute on something they actually care about. They're not here because it looks good. They're here because they chose it. That's what we look for. ...more

We have 2 engineers in San Francisco and 6 in India. The India team built the foundation of Surface. When we started, the engineering work was split across both teams. SF owned customer conversations and product decisions. India owned the backend architecture. They weren't executing someone else's vision. They were building the actual product. CQRS, event sourcing, domain driven architecture. Real systems thinking. Not quick hacks. What shocked me was the energy. These engineers didn't have to care this much. They could phone it in. Instead they're shipping features end-to-end, thinking about edge cases, refactoring code because they know it matters. One of them was literally the core developer on Astro.js. Another was architecting systems that would normally take a team of five. They were grinding. The reason we could move this fast wasn't just because they were spread out. It was because every single one of them owned what they shipped. No handoffs. No "this is someone else's problem." They built it, they tested it, they shipped it. Everyone talks to customers. SF, India, doesn't matter. When a customer has a problem, the engineer closest to it jumps in. They're not waiting for instructions. They're deciding. They're shipping. Everything combines. The SF team, the India team, the product, the customers. It all works together. We grew fast because we had engineers across two time zones who understood that pushing Surface forward means everyone owns it. That's just a really good engineering team that happened to be in two places. ...more

The pages bringing us the most traffic had nothing in common with what we were publishing. Here's what we changed: We were doing proper keyword research with search volume, difficulty scores, and competitor gap analysis, so every topic we picked had a real reason behind it. Then I sorted every page on our site by traffic, and a handful of them were doing almost all the work. Nothing we had published in months looked anything like them. We had been trying to guess which topics would work while sitting on a list of the ones that already had. A keyword tool tells you what a lot of people search for. Your own traffic tells you which of those searches actually ended up on your site. So we stopped starting from keywords and started starting from what had already worked: 1/ Pull your top pages by traffic out of Google Analytics. 2/ Compile them into one document, so the pattern across them is visible in one place. 3/ Run that through a Claude SEO skill that pulls the AEO and SEO keywords those pages already rank for. 4/ Write more in that same shape, aimed at the same buyer questions. 5/ Review every draft before it ships, because AI writing that nobody edited is how you end up with slop on your own domain. 6/ Publish, then check analytics again and build on whatever moved. The review step is the one people skip and it is the one that decides whether this compounds or wrecks your site. A model can match a structure, but it cannot tell you when a paragraph says nothing. All of it runs inside Surface, from the analytics pull through to publish. Most content plans get built from what the market searches for. Very few get built from what your own site has already proven.

when selling b2b - you swap out a no-brainer offer with nurture to close deals. just like you use shallots when you don’t have onions. it’s not ideal but that’s the only way forward. when audiences read your offer - conversion depends on how much urgency ur offer has been able to create in them. (and if they’re already in a buying journey which u cannot control) now - there’s 2 types of businesses : 1. Ones that can create a no brainer offer (either via skill or nature of business) imagine all the churn lowering tools and discount tools. they don’t charge any money upfront, they only charge you a percentage of how much they save you. this is where prospects try it out then and there -they don’t need to be nurtured a lot. ——- 2. Ones that don’t have any no brainer offer and just need the lead to buy. (most agencies and products) this is where you win deals using nurture. you send them content. you send then weekly emails, you have a great nurture instrument like a mini tool or a youtube channel or a podcast series. something where people can stay connected until they’re ready to make a purchase. ———— the best companies do both. they have no - brainer offers + a strong nurture mechanism. the 2nd best - use no brainer offers. the decent ones have nurture sequences set up - especially for high ticket deals. and the worst ones have nothing. you visit their landing page and see a sign up button or have to fuck off. climb this ladder and you’ll make money accordingly.

I built a Slack bot that debugs our production issues before any engineer even notices them. It sits on our alerts channel. The moment a monitor fires, a Claude agent picks up the alert, queries Axiom and a read-only copy of our Postgres, and posts a root-cause writeup right back in the thread. You can reply to steer the investigation, ask it for the list of impacted records, whatever you need. I fired a test alert at it just to see if the plumbing worked. Instead of parsing the alert and stopping there, it pivoted to the database on its own and surfaced a real, ongoing bug that nobody had reported. It laid out the mechanism and the blast radius over the last day, and flagged that the same thing had happened once before, months earlier, then gone quiet. Hours later a teammate hit the exact same bug by hand while testing something unrelated. By then the bot had already scoped it: the affected records, the root cause, and the fix. An agent can rip through log and database queries faster than any engineer. It pulled a full day of data and the exact impacted records in the time it takes to read the alert. But judgment is still the bottleneck: knowing which query to run, whether a number is actually a problem, what to do about it. The bot is fast hands. Someone still has to decide.
